title: ABSTRACTS: Amsterdam Benchmark Suite for the Time and Resource Analysis of Clifford+T Simulators
authors: Matthew Sutcliffe, John van de Wetering
abstract: Recent years have seen a rapid growth in literature presenting new methods for simulating non-Clifford quantum circuits with classical hardware. These methods span a range of approaches, including stabiliser decomposition and tensor contraction techniques, varying in efficiency depending on circuit class, depth, non-Clifford gate count, and other metrics. A notable limitation of this literature is the lack of a standardised approach to benchmarking, with each new paper outlining its own specification, simulating its own set of circuits on the authors' own hardware. This paper seeks to address this issue by presenting a standardised and canonical benchmark suite and infrastructure for quantifying the efficiency of non-Clifford classical simulators, with a consistent dataset of circuits and providing consistent (virtual) hardware, thereby enabling a fair comparison of results.
summary: This paper addresses the lack of standardization in benchmarking classical quantum circuit simulators by introducing the Amsterdam Benchmark Suite (ABSTRACTS). It provides a canonical framework and consistent datasets to fairly compare the time and resource efficiency of various simulation techniques for Clifford+T circuits. This infrastructure is vital for the community to accurately assess the scaling behavior of quantum simulation methods.
main_problem: The field lacks a standardized, canonical benchmark suite for fairly comparing the efficiency of classical simulators designed for non-Clifford quantum circuits.
main_result: The authors introduce the Amsterdam Benchmark Suite (ABSTRACTS), a standardized infrastructure providing consistent datasets and virtual hardware to enable fair, quantitative comparison of simulator performance.
method: The paper develops a comprehensive benchmarking framework that tests various simulation techniques (e.g., stabiliser decomposition, tensor contraction) against standardized Clifford+T circuits.
model_or_system: The focus is on simulating non-Clifford quantum circuits, specifically those involving Clifford and T gates (Clifford+T circuits), which require strong simulation techniques.
key_observables: CPU time, memory usage, and scaling patterns relative to circuit metrics like qubit count and non-Clifford gate count.
important_parameters: Circuit depth, number of non-Clifford gates (T-count), and the specific simulation technique employed (e.g., stabiliser rank $\alpha$).
main_assumptions: The performance comparison is highly dependent on the specific circuit class and the chosen metric, meaning no single simulator is universally superior.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the automated benchmarking procedure, the dashboard for result visualization, and comparisons of CPU time scaling for different simulation methods on random circuits.
paper_structure: The paper identifies the standardization gap, proposes the ABSTRACTS framework, details the benchmarking procedure, and presents comparative results to demonstrate the utility of the standardized tool.
why_interesting: It provides essential tools for assessing the computational feasibility and scaling limits of simulating complex quantum circuits, which is crucial for understanding the resource requirements of quantum algorithms.
analysis_basis: full PDF text, analyzed in chunks

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of the automated ABSTRACTS benchmarking procedure, triggered when a new simulator or circuit (class) submission is accepted into the repository.
Figure 2: The ABSTRACTS ‘dashboard’, hosted at https://mjsutcliffe99.github.io/ ABSTRACTS/, for visualisation and analysis of its benchmark results.

Figure 3: Two plots generated via the ABSTRACTS dashboard, comparing the CPU time for simulating random Clifford+T circuits with the PyZX ‘Magic Cat’ [23] stabiliser decomposition strategy and the Qiskit Aer Statevector simulator [19]. The random Clifford+T circuits are of (left) a fixed qubit count of 20, and (right) a fixed T-count (after plugged ZX-calculus simplification) of 30, respectively. Observe the difference in exponential scaling across two different metrics, showing that neither method is better than the other in all cases.

Figure 4: A comparison of (left) the heavily contextual and verbose benchmarking summary typical of papers in the literature to date, and (right) a corresponding simple and concise summary facilitated by benchmarking with ABSTRACTS. In the latter case, the relevant computational details may be found on the GitHub repository from the ABSTRACTS version alone, rather than needing to be contextualised within each paper.
Figure 5: The file structures of (left) a simulator and (right) a circuit class in the ABSTRACTS repo.
